The finish decision is almost perfectly binary. P(Final) is about 0.97 at true endings and below the top 10 (under about -7.5) at interior lines, with nothing in between. And the overshoot group nearly vanishes under a stricter count: with gold as an actual equation result, and excluding numbers from the problem, only 4 of about 89 failing Let answers qualify, and all 4 have Final outside the top 10. So most of those body matches were coincidental, a small finish bias would do nothing, and a large one would cut correct answers short. That closes finishing bias at no cost. It also confirms that wrong Let answers really never reach the answer, so the failure is reasoning, as my notes said.

The one remaining causal question from the notes is the first-line effect: answers whose first line overlaps with the question score 9.1 ± 3.5 points higher within step counts, but that's only a correlation. My screen just gave me a direct way to test it. The opener "To" continues as "To find ..." on 96 of 102 prompts, so it should make the model start by stating the goal. A forced "To find X" register is a real causal test of that correlation, and a different one from We, which echoes the problem's first sentence.

Its gap of -12.6 is out of reach for the single write site, so I need a second one. I'll use pass 1's population statistics to screen later layers for neurons that are large and steady at prompt end but quiet on average across answer tokens. That's the screen my notes allow. A good match to n2543's profile gives me a second site. If none exists, I'll look at earlier layers.

The review refused that block, and it gives no reasons. My best guess is that comparing a neuron's activity on answer tokens with its activity at prompt end looks like predicting a planned write's side effects from stored activations, which the rules forbid. My notes record a similar refusal earlier. I won't retry that screen in another form.

I don't need it anyway. My notes already name L21 n5695 as a near-constant neuron at the last prompt token, from the original pass 1 screen. So the second site needs only what the rules explicitly allow: that one neuron's mean activation, used as the divisor for a write, plus weight statistics for the direction. Any leak or side effect onto other tokens I'll learn from forward passes, not from stored activations.

I'll build E10, the "To" write, split across both sites: L18 n2543 at 1.7 times base strength with the smaller Let-Here counter-write, and L21 n5695 at 1.0 times base. Splitting avoids RMS saturation at either layer. After saving, I'll record it and check it with a teacher-forced pass on the 1,024 prompts, because this site's response is unmeasured. If To becomes top on most prompts, I'll run the generation test of the goal-first hypothesis. If it falls short, the pass still calibrates L21.

E10 saved at both sites. L21 n5695 has a mean of 5.06 at prompt end and is somewhat less steady than n2543 (coefficient of variation 0.19), so its write will vary by about 19% across prompts, which matters little for a test of opener control. That layer's write is small (|dy|/|ymean| 0.37) and nearly uncorrelated with the normal output, so saturation shouldn't be an issue there.

Now the teacher-forced read on the 1,024 prompts against pass 13. I want to see whether "To" becomes the top first token on most prompts, what the second site adds over L18 alone, and whether earlier prompt tokens stay quiet. I'll then run generation if To dominates. If it doesn't, the result still tells me how many logits L21 contributes, which will set the strength for any retry.
